doc.title: Dawoud Sabu Adeyola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 30, 2025

title: Mother's influence and ancestry
summary: His librarian mother, her education, and her interest in history and Martin Luther King day.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Let me see if I can put this into a question. Amongst your things you’ve written or people writing about you, talk about music as a spiritual force and connecting to your African ancestry. I have a couple of questions. First of all was this urge to do that, was it a family thing? Were your parents and your grandparents interested in their ancestry or was this something you found on your own?

That’s an interesting question because it is a lot of stuff in there. My mom was very much the educator. And she was a librarian. And she was somebody who had to drop out of high school as a teenager because she was ill. She had rheumatic heart and so she couldn’t finish high school. Then she got married and there were five of us. But she used to always say — she got married at 17 I think and she had five kids. I’m the second oldest. And she used to always tell us, “You got to do good in school because as soon as you guys get up to some age or some size I’m going to go back to school and I’m going to finish my education.” So we said, “Okay, Mom.” “So don’t bring no bad report cards in here.” So we had to do good in school, right? When my baby sister was about to graduate from high school and go on to college, Mom went back to school and she got her —at that time they didn’t have — they had what they call a High School Equivalency. Now they call it something else, I forget what they call it.

Yeah, G.E.D. Before G.E.D. they had what they call High School Equivalency. She got that, and then there was this college program called SEEK which was a state program. She got in that, she got a bachelors, you know, in education. And we said, “Okay Mom proved a point.” Next thing we know she’s in grad school. She wound up with a masters in Library Science and wound up working for the Erie County Library System until she was about — well her health prevented her from working past I think 64, 65. But while she was a librarian, she did a lot of stuff for history. For instance she’s the one who started Martin Luther King day before it was a national holiday she started a program in her little library. She called me up and said, “Listen I think it’s a shame that every January comes and nobody —” because she was a big birthday — she celebrated everybody’s birthday. She said, “I think it’s bad that January 15 comes around and nobody says anything about Doctor King so I’m going to have a little program here in the library, you come down and bring the boys in the band, I’m going to cook some chicken wings” and so we started doing that. And every year it got bigger and bigger and now it’s in the — I think it’s in the Kleinhans Music Hall now, it’s this huge thing you know. And she was very much interested in the Underground Railroad and stuff like that. You know she was from Georgia and remembers coming up to Buffalo on the segregated train with her mom when she was about six. So yeah, it was a kind of DNA you know, it was kind of in the blood. But as far as me personally coming up I loved the music but I thought it was tragic how many of our great musicians like Bird, like Lee Morgan and Hank Mobley and so many others man, you know Bud Powell, that had tragic life circumstances you know. And a lot of times — Fats Waller — and they died young and a lot of it had to do with their lifestyles. You know? It had to do with alcohol, it had to do with drugs. Billie Holiday, you know, Bessie Smith, so many sad stories. But then I noticed that there was another group of musicians who seemed to not have those specific problems, and they were the ones who were more spiritually oriented. You know they were — most of them were Muslim but they could be like Benny Golson was a Jehovah’s Witness I think.
